faqs.a: CAGR stands for compound annual growth rate. It is the constant yearly rate that would grow a starting value to an ending value over a given number of years, smoothing out all the ups and downs in between.
An investment that grows from 10,000 to 18,000 in 5 years has a total gain of 80%, but its CAGR is only 12.47% per year. Total gain ignores time; CAGR accounts for it.
faqs.q: CAGR vs total return: which is better?

faqs.a: No. CAGR smooths the path, so two investments with the same CAGR can have very different volatility. It also says nothing about the risk taken to achieve the growth.
faqs.q: Does a high CAGR mean a good investment?

faqs.a: Yes, when the start value, end value and period are known. That is exactly the calculation here: the growth rate implied by those three numbers.
faqs.q: Can CAGR compare a stock to a business?

faqs.a: CAGR assumes compounding and smooth growth, which fits investments. For simple year-on-year percentage changes, the average of annual rates can differ from CAGR when values fluctuate.
Yes. Take the starting and ending population, GDP or revenue and the number of years, and the same formula gives the average annual growth rate.
faqs.q: Can I use CAGR for non-money values?

cagr-calculator.formula:
CAGR = (end_value / start_value)^(1 / years) - 1
total_growth = (end_value - start_value) / start_value
howTo: Enter the starting value of the investment or metric.
Enter the number of years between them.
Read the compound annual growth rate and the total growth.
Compare different investments by their CAGR, not their raw totals.
keyFacts: CAGR is the constant annual rate that compounds a start value into an end value.
It smooths out volatility, giving one number that summarizes multi-year growth.
A 10,000 investment growing to 18,000 in 5 years has a CAGR of 12.47%, even though the total gain is 80%.
CAGR makes investments over different time periods directly comparable.
It says nothing about the path taken: two investments can share a CAGR with very different risk.

limitations: Smooths over volatility; the actual path may be bumpy.

A descriptive measure, not professional investment advice.
